hpi: {{patient_name}} is a sexually active young adult who presents with dysuria, purulent urethral discharge, and scrotal swelling. The patient admits to illicit drug use and risky sexual practices. Chlamydia trachomatis is the most common bacterial STI — an obligate intracellular pathogen. Co-infection with gonorrhea is common (40% of women, 20% of men), so empiric treatment for both is recommended even if only chlamydia is confirmed. Most cases are asymptomatic (80% women, 50% men), making the presence of overt urethritis clinically useful. First-line diagnosis is NAAT (DNA probe) on first-catch urine. Treatment: azithromycin 1g PO single dose OR doxycycline 100mg PO BID x 7 days. Sexual partners must be treated. Screen for all STIs (gonorrhea, HIV, hepatitis B/C, syphilis, HSV).
